I couldn't find one best combo. The sources I read don't give prices or tested panel pairings for most models, so I've matched units to RV sizes. Check the retailer page for current specs and prices before you buy.

**Full-time or big RV (AC, microwave, induction):**
- **EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3:** 4,096 Wh, expandable past 12 kWh, 4,000 W running and 8,000 W surge. It's the most capable and the most expensive once you add expansion batteries. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- **Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro:** 3,024 Wh, 3,000 W running and 6,000 W surge. Solar input is about 1,400 W, but reaching that takes a large, heavy panel array. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- **ALLPOWERS R4000:** 3,456 Wh LiFePO4 (rated 3,500+ cycles), 3,600 W continuous and 6,000 W peak, with a dedicated RV outlet and a 5-year warranty. It accepts up to 2,000 W of solar across three 650 W inputs, and you need panels on all three to reach that. It weighs 45 kg (about 99 lb).
  - **Price:** $1,499 at the ALLPOWERS US store. Code EXTRA12 brings it to $1,319.12. It was tested in the cart on Oct 23 and expires Nov 15.
  - **Buy:** [ALLPOWERS R4000 via Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh)
  - **Caveat:** This is the only unit where I found a current price. The source is a deal site, and the store's checkout has the final word.

**Mid-size RV or weekend camper:**
- **BLUETTI AC200L:** 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W running and 3,600 W surge. It's the value pick, and it takes a folding solar array directly without a separate charge controller. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- **Anker SOLIX F2600:** 2,560 Wh, 2,400 W running. Its solar input is lower, which matters if you camp off-grid for more than two nights.
- **Goal Zero Yeti 1500X:** 1,516 Wh. A 300 W folding panel refills it in about six hours of good summer sun.

**Solar sizing:**
- A 300–400 W folding array can refill a mid-size station in one decent summer day. Expect less in spring and fall. ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- For a big station, roof-mounted or ground-deployed panels of 800 W or more make sense. Solar input caps how fast you recharge, so a high-input unit like the R4000 or Jackery 3000 Pro helps only if you have the panel area for it.
- The EmergencyEnergy article is written for Ontario, so its sun estimates may be conservative for the US Southwest.

**My pick:** For most RVers who want AC power, I'd start with the ALLPOWERS R4000 because it has a verified price and the most solar input per dollar. If you want expandability, choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3. If you only need a smaller system, choose the Bluetti AC200L.

Tell me your RV's loads (A/C, fridge, how many days off-grid) and your budget, and I can narrow this to one unit and a panel size.
